claims.claim: Making a small payment on an old debt does not restart the clock.
claims.quote: and to start the running of a new period of time, but no such payment of itself shall revive a cause of action once barred.
claims.note: The no-revival rule concerns an already barred claim. Before the period expires, any payment by the party to be charged toward principal or interest due on a promissory note starts a new period. There is no minimum payment amount in the text.

claims.claim: Signing something on an old debt does not restart the clock.
claims.note: What the writing says matters. Section 360 allows a signed writing to evidence an acknowledgment or promise of a new or continuing contract; it does not say signing is always ineffective.

claims.claim: The applicable limit is four years.
claims.quote:
Within four years:
(a) An action upon any contract, obligation or liability founded upon an instrument in writing, except as provided in Section 336a;
claims.note: Section 337 supplies the four-year period for covered claims. The stated scope presupposes a debt subject to that period.

claims.claim: The four-year limit keeps running no matter what you pay or sign.
claims.note: Section 337(d) expressly permits extension pursuant to section 360. The draft rules out that very possibility.

claims.claim: You can safely make a payment.
claims.note: For a promissory note near the limit, a qualifying payment can start a new period. The statute does not support the assurance of safety.

claims.claim: You can safely sign a payment plan.
claims.note: A plan signed by the party to be charged may contain the acknowledgment or promise described in section 360. The source gives no blanket assurance about signing it.

flags.text: The claim that the period always keeps running conflicts with section 360's new-period rule for qualifying promissory-note payments.
The scope includes debts both near and past the limit. The draft misses the distinction between starting a new period before the bar and reviving a claim after the bar.
“No matter what you pay or sign” ignores the type of debt, what the payment covers, who pays or signs, and whether the writing contains an acknowledgment or promise.
“You can safely” directs the reader to pay or sign without regard to those conditions.
Relying on that assurance could lead the reader to start a new period by paying on a note near the limit, or to supply a signed acknowledgment or promise that weakens a limitations defense.

result.summary: The four-year period is supported for covered claims, but the assurance that paying or signing cannot affect it is not. Section 360 distinguishes a qualifying payment before expiration from payment alone after a claim is barred, and separately addresses signed acknowledgments and promises.
